replacement: Not many years after this, we come at last to the events already related: the affairs of Corcyra and Potidæa, and the incidents that served as a pretext for the present war. All these actions of the Hellenes, against each other and against the barbarian, took place in the fifty years between the retreat of Xerxes and the beginning of this war. In that time the Athenians put their empire on a firmer footing and raised their own home power to a very great height. The Lacedaemonians saw it clearly, yet opposed it only briefly and for the most part stayed inactive. They were slow by long habit to go to war unless necessity forced them, and in this case they were also hampered by wars at home. At last the growth of Athenian power could no longer be ignored, and their own confederacy came under its encroachments. Then they felt they could endure it no longer. The time had come to throw themselves heart and soul upon the hostile power and break it, if they could, by beginning the present war. They had already made up their own minds that the treaty had been broken and that the Athenians were guilty. Even so, they sent to Delphi and asked the God whether war would be well for them. As it is reported, he answered that if they put their whole strength into the war, victory would be theirs, and he promised that he himself would be with them, whether invoked or uninvoked. Still, they wished to summon their allies again and take a vote on whether it was proper to make war. The ambassadors of the confederates arrived and a congress was convened. All spoke their minds, and most of them denounced the Athenians and demanded that the war begin. The Corinthians did so in particular. Earlier they had gone through the cities one by one on their own account, urging them to vote for war, for fear that it would come too late to save Potidæa. replacement: The King listened to him and raised him up, with his son, as he was sitting with him in his arms in the most effective form of supplication. When the Lacedaemonians arrived not long afterwards, he refused to give Themistocles up for anything they could say. Instead he sent him off by land to the other sea, to Pydna in Alexander’s dominions, since Themistocles wished to go to the Persian king. There he met a merchant ship on the point of starting for Ionia. He went on board and was carried by a storm to the Athenian squadron that was blockading Naxos. In his alarm — luckily he was unknown to the people in the vessel — he told the master who he was and what he was fleeing from. He said that if the master refused to save him, he would declare that he was taking him for a bribe. Meanwhile their safety lay in letting no one leave the ship until a favorable time for sailing should arise. If the master complied with his wishes, he promised him a proper recompense. The master did as he asked, and after lying to for a day and a night out of reach of the squadron, at length arrived at Ephesus.
